newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Olympic hoteliers lose sleep over Australian bed tax.
newsitem.headline: Olympic hoteliers lose sleep over Australian bed tax.

text.p: Australian hoteliers have been rudely awoken by a new accomodation levy announced in the New South Wales state budget on Tuesday that applies only to the Olympic city of Sydney.

The new 10 percent bed tax would apply from September 1 on accommodation at hotels, motels and guest houses in Sydney's central business district and is projected to eventually raise A$64 million (US$50 million) a year.

Tourism Task Force chairman John Brown lamented the timing of the surprise tax with preparations for the year 2000 Games in full swing and warned on Wednesday that it would be costly to Olympic visitors.

"I think it is extraordinary. The Olympic Games prices will be at a premium now because of the charges that have to be laid in," he said, pointing out that agreements with the Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games (SOCOG), primarily about the restraining of room rates over the Olympic game period, would have to be reviewed.

"Only about 50 percent of hotels have signed agreements with SOCOG and I know some big corporations that are yet to sign. They have put the agreements in the drawer and said we will investigate this a lot further before we sign anything," Brown said.

The general manager of the Hotel Inter-Continental, Wolfgang Grimm, agreed the tax had been unsettling and that hoteliers could be forced to review rates to minimise the tax's effects. He said such changes were unlikely to endear Australia to overseas tourist operators.
"It could bring a lot of unrest into the situation and could mean there will be a revision of Olympic rates," Grimm said.
"It could mean that all of a sudden this very local isolated issue becomes a matter of international importance and this will not help our city."

Other hoteliers echoed similar sentiments, saying they had entered into agreements about Olympic room rates as part of their contribution to the Sydney 2000 bid and were nonplussed by the state government's latest action.

"Part of the deal with the government was we would restrain our rates and we would work with the government in controlling rates, so when the games came around we wouldn't be in a situation where rates were skyrocketing,' said Peter Tuderhope, executive assistant manager at Sydney's Regent Hotel.
"That obviously had some impact on the Olympic bid at the time. We have gone into agreements since then, maintaining that we will continue to do that, and this (tax) has been a real curve ball."
